story: In 1960, astronomers cataloged a fuzzy speck in the Tarantula Nebula named RMC 136. For decades, they wondered if it was a single impossible monster 3,000 times the mass of the Sun or a tight cluster. Groundbreaking speckle imaging and the Hubble Space Telescope eventually revealed it was a swarm of hyper-luminous giants. At its molten heart sits R136a1, a Wolf-Rayet star that smashed the long-held 150-solar-mass cosmic speed limit. Blazing millions of times brighter than our Sun, R136a1 radiates more energy in just four seconds than our Sun emits in an entire year. Yet this titan is doomed by its own brilliance. Howling radiation winds blast away over a billion times more mass every year than the Sun loses, stripping off tens of solar masses. Fusing hydrogen furiously, it is slated to shed most of its colossal bulk before collapsing into a black hole.
angle: R136a1 radiates more energy in four seconds than the Sun produces in an entire year, driving stellar winds that strip away mass a billion times faster than the Sun.
disputed: Current stellar mass: ESO (2010) reported ~265 solar masses, a 2022 Gemini South study reported ~196 solar masses, and other models report up to 291 solar masses. The script should mention that current mass estimates range between roughly 196 and nearly 300 solar masses depending on instruments and models.

Luminosity: Estimates vary from 4.68 million solar luminosities (Star Facts) to 7.24 million (Wikipedia) and up to close to 10 million solar luminosities (ESO 2010 release). The script should state it shines millions of times brighter than the Sun (between 4.7 and 10 million times).

Final fate: The 2010 ESO release raised the prospect that stars between 150 and 300 solar masses might detonate as pair-instability supernovae that completely destroy the star without leaving any remnant; later modeling indicates R136a1 will shed enough mass to collapse directly into a black hole instead. The script should frame this as a shift in theoretical models.
